questions.q: What are the three main lock granularities covered in this lesson?
options: Row, page, and table
Shared, exclusive, and update
Intent shared, intent exclusive, and intent shared-exclusive
Schema stability, schema modification, and intent
questions.explain: Granularity describes the SIZE of the resource being locked — a single row, an 8KB page, or the whole table.

questions.q: What does row-level locking give you, and what does it cost at scale?
options: Best concurrency, since unrelated rows never conflict, but more memory/CPU overhead when thousands of rows are touched in one statement
Worst concurrency, since every row lock blocks the whole table
No overhead at all, regardless of how many rows are affected
It is identical to table-level locking in every respect
questions.explain: Row locks are the most granular, giving the best concurrency, but tracking huge numbers of individual row locks has real overhead.

questions.q: What is the real cost of a table lock, even if the holding transaction only cares about a few rows?
options: Nothing else can touch any row in that table while it's held, even rows the holder never looked at
It has no real cost — table locks are always strictly better
It only blocks DDL statements, never ordinary SELECTs
It automatically converts to row locks after a few seconds
questions.explain: A table lock has the least tracking overhead but the worst concurrency, since it blocks access to the entire table regardless of which rows are actually relevant.

questions.q: Who decides which lock granularity a given statement uses?
options: SQL Server's query optimizer, automatically, based on cost estimates like expected rows touched
The developer, by specifying a GRANULARITY keyword in the statement
Whichever session connects first always gets row locks; later sessions get table locks
It's fixed per database and can never vary between statements
questions.explain: Granularity isn't chosen directly in ordinary T-SQL — the optimizer picks it based on estimated cost and table/index structure.

questions.q: Where does a page lock fall on the concurrency-vs-overhead spectrum?
options: In between row and table locks — fewer lock entries than row-level locking, but it can block unrelated rows that share the same 8KB page
It always has better concurrency than a row lock
It always has more overhead than a table lock
Page locks don't actually block any other transaction
questions.explain: A page lock covers several rows at once, trading some concurrency for reduced lock-tracking overhead compared to pure row-level locking.
